entities.name: The Biblical Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Biblical Corpus encompasses 66 canonical books (Protestant) or 73 books (Catholic/Orthodox) spanning from Genesis through Revelation, composed over roughly 1,100 years (c. 1200 BCE – 100 CE) in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Koine Greek. It includes law, history, poetry, prophecy, gospels, and epistles, and forms the foundational sacred text of both Judaism and Christianity — the two most historically influential religious traditions in Western civilization.

The canon emerged through centuries of deliberate selection. The Jewish Torah (Five Books of Moses) was codified during the Babylonian Exile (586–538 BCE), when survival without a Temple made written scripture central to identity. The Hebrew Bible was largely canonized by 200 BCE. The New Testament canon was settled by the Council of Carthage (397 CE) after three centuries of debate. The Septuagint (Greek translation, c. 250 BCE) made the Hebrew scriptures accessible across the Mediterranean world and became the Bible of early Christianity.

The Biblical Corpus has been translated into over 3,500 languages — more than any other work in human history. Its narratives have shaped the moral imagination of three billion people across 2,000 years. Western legal concepts of covenant, individual rights before God, and justice all trace philosophical roots to Biblical precedent. Every major artistic tradition of the Western world — from Byzantine mosaics to Rembrandt to Handel's Messiah — draws directly from its imagery and stories.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Biblical Corpus has shaped Western civilization through its influence on Christianity and Judaism, with an estimated 2.4 billion adherents worldwide, and its contents have been translated into over 2,000 languages, contributing to the development of art, literature, philosophy, and ethics.
